content: 1. The rapid deterioration of insecticidal nets, loss of nets, and population growth necessitate the establishment of continuous distribution channels to maintain effective malaria control post-campaign. 2. Achieving and sustaining universal coverage with long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) is critical for malaria control, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). 3. Operational weaknesses, such as logistical challenges and incomplete data collection, hinder the effective distribution of LLINs through antenatal care (ANC) and child immunization services. 4. Stockouts of LLINs at healthcare facilities are common and disrupt smooth distribution operations. These stockouts are often caused by inadequate supply forecasting, logistical issues, and poor data collection systems. 5. Many countries lack clear guidelines for addressing stockouts or systems that allow local health workers to request additional LLINs when needed. 6. Data collection on LLIN distribution at healthcare facilities is often incomplete and not utilized for planning purposes. 7. Training of health workers on the importance of providing LLINs during the first antenatal care visit is frequently suboptimal, leading to missed opportunities for distribution. 8. The strategy of distributing LLINs to pregnant women through antenatal services and to infants through immunization services is effective in areas with high attendance rates for these services and robust supply-chain logistics. 9. Logistical challenges, including transportation, storage, and distribution, must be carefully considered, especially during campaigns or outreach activities, due to the bulky nature of LLINs. 10. Immunization programs in malaria-endemic countries should explore synergies with malaria control programs to enhance the effectiveness of both initiatives. 11. Joint planning for training, logistics, and data collection is essential for the successful implementation of LLIN distribution programs. 12. Intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi) with antimalarials leverages the protective effects of chemoprevention against malaria while minimizing interference with the development of natural immunity. 13. IPTi involves administering a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medication to infants at scheduled intervals during routine immunization visits, regardless of malaria infection status. 14. Coordinating IPTi delivery with routine immunization visits can significantly increase coverage, but progress in adopting and implementing IPTi has been slow. 15. WHO recommends the co-administration of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) IPTi with DTP2, DTP3, and measles immunizations in sub-Saharan Africa in areas with moderate-to-high malaria transmission and low SP resistance. 16. Programs implementing SP-IPTi should regularly monitor and evaluate its impact on immunization services and performance, strengthen pharmacovigilance systems, and conduct surveillance of parasite resistance to SP. 17. IPTi is intended to complement, not replace, existing malaria control measures such as prompt diagnosis and treatment, LLIN use, and indoor residual spraying. 18. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) is recommended in areas of highly seasonal malaria transmission, particularly in the Sahel sub-region, where drug resistance to SP is low. 19. SMC involves administering a complete treatment course of amodiaquine plus SP to children aged 3–59 months at monthly intervals during the malaria transmission season, up to a maximum of four doses. 20. SMC is typically delivered through mass campaigns using trained community health workers, with limited experience in health facility-based or immunization outreach-based delivery. 21. Joint planning with malaria programs is necessary to assess the feasibility of delivering SMC via immunization outreach, considering the country context. 22. SMC and IPTi should not be administered simultaneously. In areas targeted for SMC, IPTi should not be used. 23. Deworming drugs are often administered to pregnant women and children in developing countries to combat soil-transmitted helminths (STH), which impair nutritional status in multiple ways.
